title: One man for the people (John 11:45–57)
hook: the council plots; Caiaphas says it's better one man die

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus wept at a tomb, and Lazarus walked out, still wrapped in grave clothes. Your line was loose him, let him go.

A room, worried people, and someone saying the hard, practical thing out loud. After Lazarus walks out of the tomb, many who saw it believe. Some go to Jerusalem and report what happened, and the chief priests and leaders call an emergency meeting of the council. Their question is frightened, and very human: "What do we? for this man doeth many miracles." They're not debating whether the miracle happened. They're asking what it will cost them.

First, the pressure on the room. Judea was under Roman occupation. Rome let the temple and its leaders keep a measure of authority, as long as there was order. Crowds, excitement, talk of a king: that was exactly what Rome crushed. The council says it plainly: "If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation." Their fear wasn't imaginary. Decades later, Roman armies did destroy the temple. Then the high priest that year, Caiaphas, speaks: "Ye know nothing at all, nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not." Expedient means useful, the practical choice. One life traded for many: an old logic, sacrifice one to keep the peace. And then John does something remarkable. He says Caiaphas spoke better than he knew. Being high priest, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, "and not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad." The same sentence, heard two ways. Caiaphas meant politics. John hears the gospel in it. From that day, John says, they made plans. Jesus withdraws to a town called Ephraim, near the wilderness. Passover is near, and the whole city wonders: will he come to the feast? It was Rome that would carry out the execution. But the road toward it begins in a frightened room.
screen: then, large: `ONE MAN SHOULD DIE FOR THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who makes hard decisions for others, a mayor, a head of state, a school principal, a hospital director, a manager at work, and imagine the weight of their room: competing fears, real dangers, people who'll be hurt either way. You don't have to agree with them; just picture them as people under pressure. If you pray, pray for them by name, for wisdom and courage, and that no one is sacrificed for convenience; if not, hold them in mind with honesty and fairness.
Caiaphas. The high priest who said one man should die for the people, which John hears as an unknowing prophecy of Jesus's death.
Your line: for the nation. One sentence, heard two ways: politics and prophecy. Day six hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Many churches pray for those in authority in their regular services; Christians read Caiaphas's words as an unknowing prophecy that Jesus would die for many.

fork.reveal: "it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people." John hears in it more than Caiaphas meant.

original.note: Greek: it is better, it's to our advantage. The King James says expedient.

what it means: a frightened council under Roman occupation makes a practical, terrible choice: one life to protect the many.
what a scholar hears: John reads Caiaphas's words as unknowing prophecy, given, John says, because he was high priest that year.

chat.says: Why would the leaders want Jesus stopped right after he raised someone?
options: John says they feared Rome would take their place and nation if crowds followed him.
John says they doubted the miracle and thought Lazarus had never really died.
John says they wanted his power for themselves and planned to take it from him.
chat.meaning: Under Roman pressure, the council feared losing their place and nation. Caiaphas said one man should die for the people, and John hears a prophecy in it.

council.meaning: the leaders' ruling body, called to an emergency meeting

Ephraim.meaning: a town near the wilderness where Jesus withdrew

Judea.meaning: the region around Jerusalem, then under Roman occupation
